claim: Synaptotagmin1 (Syt1) forms Ca2+-sensitive ring-like oligomers on membranes containing acidic lipids.
source: Previously, we showed that synaptotagmin1 (Syt1) forms Ca2+-sensitive ring-like oligomers on membranes containing acidic lipids and proposed a potential role in regulating neurotransmitter release (Zanetti et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Zanetti et al., 2016).

claim: Syt1 assembles into ring-like oligomers in solution when triggered by polyphosphates (PIP2 and ATP) and magnesium ions (Mg2+).
source: Here, we report that Syt1 assembles into similar ring-like oligomers in solution when triggered by naturally occurring polyphosphates (PIP2 and ATP) and magnesium ions (Mg2+).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including electron microscopy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy.

claim: Soluble Syt1 rings were observed by electron microscopy.
source: These soluble Syt1 rings were observed by electron microscopy and independently demonstrated and quantified using fluorescence correlation spectroscopy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electron microscopy presented in the manuscript.

claim: Soluble Syt1 rings were independently demonstrated and quantified using fluorescence correlation spectroscopy.
source: These soluble Syt1 rings were observed by electron microscopy and independently demonstrated and quantified using fluorescence correlation spectroscopy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence correlation spectroscopy presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oligomerization is triggered when polyphosphates bind to the polylysine patch in C2B domain.
source: Oligomerization is triggered when polyphosphates bind to the polylysine patch in C2B domain and is stabilized by Mg2+, which neutralizes the Ca2+-binding aspartic acids that likely contribute to the C2B interface in the oligomer.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutations in the polylysine patch prevent oligomerization.

claim: Syt1 oligomerization is stabilized by Mg2+, which neutralizes the Ca2+-binding aspartic acids that likely contribute to the C2B interface in the oligomer.
source: Oligomerization is triggered when polyphosphates bind to the polylysine patch in C2B domain and is stabilized by Mg2+, which neutralizes the Ca2+-binding aspartic acids that likely contribute to the C2B interface in the oligomer.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Mg2+ increases ring density and that neutralizing Ca2+-binding aspartic acids stabilizes rings even without Mg2+.

claim: Ring-like polymerization is an intrinsic property of Syt1 with reasonable affinity.
source: Overall, our data show that ring-like polymerization is an intrinsic property of Syt1 with reasonable affinity that can be triggered by the vesicle docking C2B-PIP2 interaction and raise the possibility that Syt1 rings could pre-form on the synaptic vesicle to facilitate docking.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing ring formation in solution and calculated binding affinity.

claim: Syt1 ring formation can be triggered by the vesicle docking C2B-PIP2 interaction.
source: Overall, our data show that ring-like polymerization is an intrinsic property of Syt1 with reasonable affinity that can be triggered by the vesicle docking C2B-PIP2 interaction and raise the possibility that Syt1 rings could pre-form on the synaptic vesicle to facilitate docking.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that PIP2 triggers ring formation.

claim: Syt1 rings could pre-form on the synaptic vesicle to facilitate docking.
source: Overall, our data show that ring-like polymerization is an intrinsic property of Syt1 with reasonable affinity that can be triggered by the vesicle docking C2B-PIP2 interaction and raise the possibility that Syt1 rings could pre-form on the synaptic vesicle to facilitate docking.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Synaptic vesicle (SV) fusion at the neuronal synapse is mediated by the SNARE complex.
source: Synaptic vesicle (SV) fusion at the neuronal synapse is mediated by the SNARE (soluble NSF attachment protein receptor) complex, whose assembly is chaperoned by several other proteins to achieve precision and synchronicity of neurotransmitter release (Südhof, 2013; Söllner et al., 1993a, 1993b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: SNARE assembly is chaperoned by several proteins including Munc18, Munc13, complexin, synaptotagmin1 (Syt1), α-SNAP, and NSF.
source: These include Munc18, Munc13, complexin, synaptotagmin1 (Syt1), α-SNAP, and NSF (Südhof, 2013; Südhof and Rothman, 2009; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012; Rizo and Xu, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Syt1 is the primary calcium (Ca2+) sensor that triggers rapid, synchronous neurotransmitter release after Ca2+ entry into the pre-synaptic terminal following an action potential.
source: SV-associated protein Syt1 is of special interest because it is the primary calcium (Ca2+) sensor that triggers the rapid, synchronous neurotransmitter release after Ca2+ are admitted into the pre-synaptic terminal following an action potential (Brose et al., 1992; Fernández-Chacón et al., 2001; Geppert et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The Ca2+-induced reorientation of the cytoplasmic C2 domains (C2A and C2B) of Syt1 into the membrane is the driving force behind neurotransmitter release.
source: It is well-established that the Ca2+-induced reorientation of the cytoplasmic C2 domains (C2A and C2B) of Syt1 into the membrane is driving force behind this process (Rhee et al., 2005; Paddock et al., 2011; Hui et al., 2006; Krishnakumar et al., 2013), but the precise molecular details are still unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Under resting conditions, Syt1 is involved in pre-fusion docking and priming of SVs to the plasma membrane (PM).
source: Under resting conditions, Syt1 is also involved in pre-fusion docking and priming of SVs to the plasma membrane (PM).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature in the following sentences.

claim: Syt1 docking involves the interaction of the polybasic patch of C2B domain with negatively charged phospholipids like PIP2 and PS in the PM.
source: This involves the interaction of the polybasic patch of C2B domain with the negatively charged phospholipids, like phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) and phosphatidylserine (PS) in the PM (Wang et al., 2011; Bai et al., 2004; Honigmann et al., 2013; Parisotto et al., 2012; Pérez-Lara et al., 2016; Martin, 2015), and independent but concurrent binding to the t-SNAREs, Syntaxin and SNAP-25 (Zhou et al., 2015; de Wit et al., 2009; Kedar et al., 2015; Mohrmann et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Syt1 binds independently but concurrently to t-SNAREs, Syntaxin and SNAP-25.
source: This involves the interaction of the polybasic patch of C2B domain with the negatively charged phospholipids, like phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) and phosphatidylserine (PS) in the PM (Wang et al., 2011; Bai et al., 2004; Honigmann et al., 2013; Parisotto et al., 2012; Pérez-Lara et al., 2016; Martin, 2015), and independent but concurrent binding to the t-SNAREs, Syntaxin and SNAP-25 (Zhou et al., 2015; de Wit et al., 2009; Kedar et al., 2015; Mohrmann et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Prior to Ca2+ entry, the SNARE complex is approximately half-zippered but unable to complete its zippering to drive fusion.
source: Also, multiple lines of evidence (Hua and Charlton, 1999; Walter et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014; Giraudo et al., 2006) imply that prior to the entry of Ca2+, the SNARE complex is approximately half-zippered but unable to complete its zippering to drive fusion and Syt1, along with Complexin, might be involved in maintaining this pre-fusion activated state.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Syt1, along with Complexin, might be involved in maintaining the pre-fusion activated state of half-zippered SNAREs.
source: Also, multiple lines of evidence (Hua and Charlton, 1999; Walter et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014; Giraudo et al., 2006) imply that prior to the entry of Ca2+, the SNARE complex is approximately half-zippered but unable to complete its zippering to drive fusion and Syt1, along with Complexin, might be involved in maintaining this pre-fusion activated state.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from cited literature.

claim: Syt1 self-assembles into ~30 nm sized rings (~17 copies of Syt1) on lipid surfaces.
source: We found that Syt1 self-assembles into ~30 nm sized rings (~17 copies of Syt1) on lipid surfaces, which disassemble upon binding Ca2+ in the physiologically-relevant range (Wang et al., 2014; Zanetti et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Syt1 rings on lipid surfaces disassemble upon binding Ca2+ in the physiologically-relevant range.
source: We found that Syt1 self-assembles into ~30 nm sized rings (~17 copies of Syt1) on lipid surfaces, which disassemble upon binding Ca2+ in the physiologically-relevant range (Wang et al., 2014; Zanetti et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ring-like oligomers are a conserved structural feature of many C2 domain proteins.
source: While there is as yet no direct evidence that such rings exist in vivo at the SV-PM junction, nonetheless striking genetic and biochemical correlations provided by the ring structure (Wang et al., 2014; Zanetti et al., 2016) and the fact that the ring-like oligomers are a conserved structural feature of many C2 domain proteins (Zanetti et al., 2016) strongly support the overall hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the presence of 50 µM PIP2-diC4, Syt1C2AB readily assembles into ring-like oligomers in solution.
source: Negative stain analysis showed that in the presence of 50 µM PIP2-diC4, Syt1C2AB readily assembles into ring-like oligomers in solution (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The density of soluble Syt1C2AB ring oligomers is ~5 rings/µm2.
source: The density (~5 rings/ µm2) and the dimension (outer diameter between 18–44 nm with an average size of ~32 nm) of these soluble ring oligomers were very similar to the ring oligomers formed on the lipid surface (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electron microscopy data.

claim: The outer diameter of soluble Syt1C2AB ring oligomers is between 18–44 nm with an average size of ~32 nm.
source: The density (~5 rings/ µm2) and the dimension (outer diameter between 18–44 nm with an average size of ~32 nm) of these soluble ring oligomers were very similar to the ring oligomers formed on the lipid surface (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Soluble Syt1C2AB ring oligomers contain 12–26 copies of Syt1 molecule, with an average of ~17 copies.
source: Based on the helical indexing of the Syt1C2AB tubes (Wang et al., 2014), we estimate that this corresponds to 12–26 copies of Syt1 molecule, with an average of ~17 copies of Syt1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from helical indexing data cited from prior work.

claim: Soluble Syt1C2AB rings are abundant and stable under physiological buffer conditions.
source: Notably, the soluble Syt1C2AB rings are abundant and stable under physiological buffer conditions, unlike the sparse density observed on lipid monolayers (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with cited prior work.

claim: Circular oligomerization is an intrinsic property of Syt1 C2 domains.
source: This suggests that circular oligomerization is an intrinsic property of Syt1 C2 domains, but hindered by the low concentration of the protein on the lipid monolayer surface under these conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that rings form more abundantly in solution than on lipid surfaces.

claim: IP3 (50 µM) induces ring oligomerization of Syt1C2AB similar to PIP2.
source: Similar ring oligomers were observed with PIP2 analogues like inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3, 50 µM) (Figure 1D) suggesting it was not a unique property of PIP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ATP at physiological concentration (1 mM Mg-ATP) induces ring-like oligomers of Syt1C2AB.
source: As with soluble PIP2 and its analogues, we detected ring-like oligomers of Syt1C2AB (Figure 1E) at physiological concentration of ATP (1 mM Mg-ATP), with density (~5 rings/µm2) comparable to soluble PIP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 1 mM adenosine diphosphate (ADP) induces similar ring oligomers of Syt1C2AB.
source: Similar ring oligomers were also observed with 1 mM adenosine diphosphate (ADP) suggesting that it is a shared property of polyvalent anions (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: No oligomeric structures were observed in the absence of polyvalent anions.
source: No oligomeric structures were observed in the absence of polyvalent anions and the density of the rings was drastically reduced (~5 rings/µm2 to ~0.4 rings/µm2) when the polybasic region of C2B was mutated (K326A/K327A) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The density of Syt1C2AB rings was drastically reduced (~5 rings/µm2 to ~0.4 rings/µm2) when the polybasic region of C2B was mutated (K326A/K327A).
source: No oligomeric structures were observed in the absence of polyvalent anions and the density of the rings was drastically reduced (~5 rings/µm2 to ~0.4 rings/µm2) when the polybasic region of C2B was mutated (K326A/K327A) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The direct molecular interaction of polyanions with the C2B polybasic motif produces the Syt1 ring-like oligomers.
source: This suggests that the known direct molecular interaction of polyanions with the C2B polybasic motif (Park et al., 2012; Bai et al., 2004) and not a charge shielding effect, produces the Syt1 ring-like oligomers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutation data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Magnesium ions (Mg2+) are an important co-factor in stabilizing the Syt1C2AB rings in solution.
source: Magnesium ions (Mg2+) were also found to be an important co-factor in stabilizing the Syt1C2AB rings in solution (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The number of Syt1C2AB ring oligomers observed were substantially reduced (~60% reduction) when Mg2+ was completely excluded (using Na-ATP or Na-PIP2).
source: The number of Syt1C2AB ring oligomers observed were substantially reduced (~60% reduction) when Mg2+ was completely excluded (using Na-ATP or Na-PIP2) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mg2+ was not required to assemble the Syt1C2AB ring oligomers on acidic lipid surfaces.
source: Given that the Mg2+ was not required to assemble the Syt1C2AB ring oligomers on acidic lipid surfaces (in fact Mg2+ lowered the number of rings formed on lipid surfaces), it appears that Mg2+ plays an independent but auxiliary role in the formation of Syt1C2AB ring oligomers in solution.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with prior observations on lipid surfaces.

claim: Mg2+ plays an independent but auxiliary role in the formation of Syt1C2AB ring oligomers in solution.
source: Given that the Mg2+ was not required to assemble the Syt1C2AB ring oligomers on acidic lipid surfaces (in fact Mg2+ lowered the number of rings formed on lipid surfaces), it appears that Mg2+ plays an independent but auxiliary role in the formation of Syt1C2AB ring oligomers in solution.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of solution and lipid surface data.

claim: The soluble Syt1C2AB rings (triggered with ATP and Mg2+) were not stable under glycerol density gradient experimental conditions.
source: However, the soluble rings were not stable under these experimental conditions and could be isolated only after mild fixation (0.01% glutaraldehyde) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The soluble Syt1C2AB rings could be isolated after mild fixation (0.01% glutaraldehyde).
source: However, the soluble rings were not stable under these experimental conditions and could be isolated only after mild fixation (0.01% glutaraldehyde) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The specific interaction of polyvalent anions to the conserved lysine residues within the C2B polybasic motif triggers the Syt1 ring-like oligomer formation.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that the specific interaction of the polyvalent anions to the conserved lysine residues within the C2B polybasic motif triggers the Syt1 ring-like oligomer formation and the resultant oligomers are stabilized by Mg2+.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on mutations and Mg2+ effects.

claim: Syt1 ring oligomers are stabilized by Mg2+.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that the specific interaction of the polyvalent anions to the conserved lysine residues within the C2B polybasic motif triggers the Syt1 ring-like oligomer formation and the resultant oligomers are stabilized by Mg2+.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on Mg2+ effects.

claim: In the presence of ATP and Mg2+, the temporal variations in the fluorescence intensity of Alexa488 and Alexa647 labels followed a similar pattern.
source: In the presence of ATP and Mg2+, the temporal variations in the fluorescence intensity of Alexa488 and Alexa647 labels followed a similar pattern, indicating that part of Syt1C2AB-Alexa488 and Syt1C2AB-Alexa647 molecules move in or out the focal volume concurrently (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The cross-correlation function was larger than one at short time intervals in the presence of ATP and Mg2+.
source: Also, the cross-correlation function was larger than one at short time intervals (Figure 3A), indicating that a portion of the two fluorophores diffused together that is, they were in the same diffusional object.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A portion of the two fluorophores (Alexa488 and Alexa647) diffused together in the presence of ATP and Mg2+, indicating they were in the same diffusional object.
source: Also, the cross-correlation function was larger than one at short time intervals (Figure 3A), indicating that a portion of the two fluorophores diffused together that is, they were in the same diffusional object.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cross-correlation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: FCS data are consistent with the formation of Syt1C2AB oligomers in solution in the presence of ATP and Mg2+.
source: Overall, these data were consistent with the formation of Syt1C2AB oligomers in solution.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FCS data presented.

claim: No cross correlation was observed in the absence of ATP and Mg2+.
source: Further, we observed no cross correlation (Figure 3B) in the absence of ATP and Mg2+, implying that these structures are not random association of Syt1C2AB molecules, but are ATP-derived oligomers of Syt1C2AB.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Syt1C2AB oligomers are not random associations but are ATP-derived oligomers.
source: Further, we observed no cross correlation (Figure 3B) in the absence of ATP and Mg2+, implying that these structures are not random association of Syt1C2AB molecules, but are ATP-derived oligomers of Syt1C2AB.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of FCS data with and without ATP/Mg2+.

claim: The auto correlation function of Syt1C2AB in the presence of ATP and Mg2+ was best fitted using the two-component translational diffusion model with a triplet state correction.
source: We found that they could be best fitted using the two-component translational diffusion model with a triplet state correction (Equation 1) and determined two diffusion coefficients corresponding to the Syt1C2AB monomers and oligomers.
evidence: The claim is supported by FCS data analysis.

claim: The major component (~80%) of Syt1C2AB in solution showed fast diffusion time (~600 µs) corresponding to monomers.
source: The major component (~80%) showed fast diffusion time (~600 µs) possibly corresponding to the monomers and a smaller fraction (~20%) had a slow diffusion time of ~4000 µs consistent with Syt1C2AB oligomers (Figure 3C, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FCS data shown in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: A smaller fraction (~20%) of Syt1C2AB in solution had a slow diffusion time of ~4000 µs consistent with Syt1C2AB oligomers.
source: The major component (~80%) showed fast diffusion time (~600 µs) possibly corresponding to the monomers and a smaller fraction (~20%) had a slow diffusion time of ~4000 µs consistent with Syt1C2AB oligomers (Figure 3C, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FCS data shown in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: Syt1C2AB formed oligomers in solution when triggered with ATP and Mg2+.
source: These data indicated that Syt1C2AB indeed formed oligomers in solution when triggered with ATP and Mg2+.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FCS data analysis.

claim: In the absence of ATP and Mg2+, the auto correlation function of Syt1C2AB could be best fitted with the one component translational diffusion model with triplet state correction.
source: In contrast, in the absence of ATP and Mg2+, the auto correlation function could be best fitted with the one component translational diffusion model with triplet state correction (Equation 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by FCS data analysis.

claim: The diffusion time obtained in the absence of ATP and Mg2+ (~600 µs for both channels) was similar to the diffusion time of the monomeric component.
source: The diffusion time (τd) obtained (~600 µs for both channels) were similar to the diffusion time of the monomeric component obtained in the two component diffusion model, confirming that no oligomeric structure is formed in the absence of Mg2+ and ATP (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FCS data shown in Table 1.

claim: No oligomeric structure is formed in the absence of Mg2+ and ATP.
source: The diffusion time (τd) obtained (~600 µs for both channels) were similar to the diffusion time of the monomeric component obtained in the two component diffusion model, confirming that no oligomeric structure is formed in the absence of Mg2+ and ATP (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FCS data shown in Table 1.

claim: For the polylysine mutant (K326A/K327A) in the presence of ATP and Mg2+, the autocorrelation function was best described with one-component diffusion model with a diffusion time of 599 ± 50 μs and a diffusion coefficient of 72 ± 7 μm2/s.
source: For this mutant, in the presence of ATP and Mg2+, the autocorrelation function was best described with one-component diffusion model with a diffusion time of 599 ± 50 μs and a diffusion coefficient of 72 ± 7 μm2/s, which are similar to the property of a Syt1 monomer (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by FCS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The probability of forming Syt1 oligomeric structures is significantly decreased when the polylysine patch on C2B domain was altered.
source: These data are consistent with the EM analysis that the probability of forming Syt1 oligomeric structures is significantly decreased when the polylysine patch on C2B domain was altered.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FCS data on the polylysine mutant.

claim: Similar oligomers were formed with PIP2-diC4 and Mg2+ as confirmed by autocorrelation (diffusion time) and cross-correlation analysis.
source: We also tested and confirmed that similar oligomers were formed with PIP2-diC4 and Mg2+ using both autocorrelation (diffusion time) and cross-correlation analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by FCS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The average copy number (N) of Syt1 in the oligomers is ~16 ± 2.
source: Combining Equations 4–6, we estimate the average copy number (N) of Syt1 in the oligomers to be ~16 ± 2.
evidence: The claim is calculated from FCS data using mathematical equations.

claim: The estimated copy number from FCS (~16 ± 2) perfectly matches with the estimated copies of Syt1 (~17 copies) in the ring-like oligomers from the EM analysis.
source: This perfectly matches with the estimated copies of Syt1 (~17 copies) in the ring-like oligomers from the EM analysis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of FCS and EM data.

claim: The average hydrodynamic radius of Syt1C2AB monomer is ~r = 3.1±0.2 nm.
source: We estimate an average hydrodynamic radius of ~r = 3.1±0.2 nm for the monomer and ~ (r + a)=24 ± 3 nm for Syt1 oligomer.
evidence: The claim is calculated from FCS diffusion data using the Stokes-Einstein equation.

claim: The average hydrodynamic radius of Syt1 oligomer is ~ (r + a)=24 ± 3 nm.
source: We estimate an average hydrodynamic radius of ~r = 3.1±0.2 nm for the monomer and ~ (r + a)=24 ± 3 nm for Syt1 oligomer.
evidence: The claim is calculated from FCS diffusion data using the torus model.

claim: The hydrodynamic radius values are in line with the dimension of Syt1C2AB monomer (~4.3 nm from X-ray crystallography) and ring oligomer (~32 nm from the EM analysis).
source: Both of these values are in line with the dimension of Syt1C2AB monomer (~4.3 nm from X-ray crystallography [Fuson et al., 2007]) and ring oligomer (~32 nm from the EM analysis).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of FCS-derived hydrodynamic radii with structural data from X-ray crystallography and EM.

claim: Syt1 oligomers observed in FCS analysis are the same circular oligomers visualized by EM.
source: Overall, the data suggest that Syt1 oligomers observed in FCS analysis are the same circular oligomers visualized by EM, given the molecular properties of both are perfectly aligned.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the agreement between FCS and EM data.

claim: The affinity constant (KD) for the Syt1C2AB monomers to assemble into the oligomers was estimated to be ~1 ± 0.3 µM.
source: From Equation 10, the affinity constant (KD) for the Syt1C2AB monomers to assemble into the oligomers was estimated to be ~1 ± 0.3 µM.
evidence: The claim is calculated from FCS data using mathematical equations.

claim: The free energy for Syt1C2AB oligomerization is ~−13.8 kBT for a monomer and ~−220 kBT for the oligomer with 16 copies of Syt1C2AB.
source: This corresponds to a free energy of ~−13.8 kBT for a monomer and ~−220 kBT for the oligomer with 16 copies of Syt1C2AB.
evidence: The claim is calculated from the affinity constant.

claim: Syt1 ring oligomers could reasonably assemble under the physiological conditions when triggered by naturally occurring polyphosphates.
source: This suggests that Syt1 ring oligomers could reasonably assemble under the physiological conditions when triggered by naturally occurring polyphosphates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the calculated affinity constant.

claim: Syt1C2AB ring oligomers assembled on the membrane surface are sensitive to Ca2+ and are rapidly disrupted by Ca2+ wash at physiological concentrations.
source: Syt1C2AB ring oligomers assembled on the membrane surface are sensitive to Ca2+ and are rapidly disrupted by Ca2+ wash at physiological concentrations (Wang et al., 2014; Zanetti et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Ca2+ sensitivity of membrane-bound Syt1 rings maps to the Ca2+ binding to the C2B domain and the subsequent insertion of the flanking aliphatic residues into the membrane.
source: This sensitivity maps to the Ca2+ binding to the C2B domain and the subsequent insertion of the flanking aliphatic residues into the membrane (Zanetti et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The soluble Syt1C2AB rings are insensitive to Ca2+ treatment.
source: In line with this, we find that the soluble Syt1C2AB rings are insensitive to Ca2+ treatment (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Syt1C2AB assembled into soluble ring-like oligomers in the presence of Ca2+/ATP similar to those observed with ATP and Mg2+.
source: Negative stain EM analysis showed the Syt1C2AB assembled into soluble ring-like oligomers in the presence of Ca2+/ATP similar to those observed with ATP and Mg2+ (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ca2+ was slightly better than Mg2+ in stabilizing the ring oligomers across the concentration range (0.25–1 mM) tested.
source: In fact, Ca2+ was slightly better in stabilizing the ring oligomers across the concentration range (0.25–1 mM) tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oligomeric structures were detected with ATP and Ca2+ in the FCS analysis, and the diffusional properties of the oligomeric component was similar to that observed with ATP and Mg2+.
source: Similarly, we detected the presence of oligomeric structures with ATP and Ca2+ in the FCS analysis, and the diffusional properties of the oligomeric component was similar to that observed with ATP and Mg2+ (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FCS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Ca2+-induced membrane interaction of the C2B domain is essential for the dissociation of the Syt1 ring oligomers following the Ca2+ influx.
source: Hence, we conclude that the Ca2+-induced membrane interaction of the C2B domain is essential for the dissociation of the Syt1 ring oligomers following the Ca2+ influx.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that soluble rings are insensitive to Ca2+ while membrane-bound rings are sensitive.

claim: Neutralizing the Ca2+ coordinating aspartic acids of the C2B domain (Syt13A, D309A/D363A/D365A) stabilized the soluble ring oligomers.
source: Remarkably, neutralizing the Ca2+ coordinating aspartic acids of the C2B domain (Syt13A, D309A/D363A/D365A) stabilized the soluble ring oligomers.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on the Syt13A mutant.

claim: Syt13A formed stable ring oligomers in the absence of divalent cations (with Na.ATP), with density comparable to those assembled with ATP and Mg2+.
source: In fact, Syt13A formed stable ring oligomers in the absence of divalent cations (with Na.ATP), with density comparable to those assembled with ATP and Mg2+ (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: C2B Ca2+ loops are involved in the ring oligomer formation.
source: This supports the idea that C2B Ca2+ loops are involved the ring oligomer formation (Wang et al., 2014) and Mg2+ stabilizes the ring oligomers by charge shielding effect that is by reducing the electrostatic repulsion between the Syt1 monomers by
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Syt13A mutant data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mg2+ stabilizes the ring oligomers by charge shielding effect, reducing the electrostatic repulsion between the Syt1 monomers.
